sheet.howExamined: M4 (calculator, 2 hours, 100 marks). An equation with algebraic denominators is set on 14 of the 15 papers from 2018 to Summer 2026, always among the last four questions, for 6 to 8 marks; six of the seven since November 2022 asked for answers to 2 decimal places, so the quadratic goes to the formula. noteBlocks.caption: Each fraction is multiplied top and bottom by the bracket it lacks, so both end over (x + 2)(x + 7) with their values unchanged.

noteBlocks.md: In the drawing, each fraction is multiplied top and bottom by the bracket it is missing. Multiplying the top and the bottom by the same thing is multiplying by 1, so neither fraction changes value, and now both are counted in the same pieces.

Two different linear brackets, such as $x+2$ and $x+7$, share no factor, so the smallest denominator both divide into is their product. Leave it as brackets: expanding it earns nothing, and the brackets are what you may need later, to cancel or to clear an equation.

steps.decision: The brackets share no factor, so the common denominator is their product, left as brackets.
Each top is multiplied by the bracket its own denominator was missing, exactly as in the drawing.
Expand each bracket on its own: the 4 and the 3 multiply both terms inside.
Collect like terms: $4x+3x=7x$ and $28+6=34$. The denominator stays as brackets.

noteBlocks.title: Adding Algebraic Fractions
noteBlocks.why: The same move at writing speed on more pairs of fractions, subtraction included. Watch it once, then answer the checks without going back.

noteBlocks.prompt: What is the common denominator for $\frac{1}{x+3} + \frac{1}{x-5}$?
noteBlocks.explain: Each fraction has to be rewritten over something its own bracket divides into, as step 1 of See it used $(x+2)(x+7)$. Two different brackets share no factor, so that is their product, $(x+3)(x-5)$. Adding them to $2x-2$ gives something neither divides, and $x+3$ alone leaves the second fraction out.

twin.prompt: What is the common denominator for $\frac{1}{x+6} + \frac{1}{x-2}$?
twin.explain: Two different brackets share no factor, so the common denominator is their product, $(x+6)(x-2)$. Adding them gives $2x+4$, which neither bracket divides, and one bracket alone leaves the other fraction out.

optionNotes.why: Adding the two bottoms looks like adding fractions, but neither x + 6 nor x − 2 divides into 2x + 4, so neither fraction can be rewritten over it.
Keeping one of the brackets is tempting, but x + 6 does not divide into x − 2, so the first fraction cannot join it.
Adding the two bottoms feels like adding the fractions, but neither bracket divides into 2x − 2, so neither fraction can be rewritten over it.
Keeping the bracket that is already there is tempting, but x − 5 does not divide into x + 3, so the second fraction cannot join it.

noteBlocks.prompt: Over $(x+6)(x+1)$, what is the collected numerator of $\frac{3}{x+6}+\frac{2}{x+1}$?
noteBlocks.explain: Each top is multiplied by the bracket it lacks, as step 2 of See it did: the 3 over $x+6$ needs $(x+1)$, and the 2 over $x+1$ needs $(x+6)$. So $3(x+1)+2(x+6)=5x+15$. Using each fraction's own bracket gives $5x+20$, and multiplying only the $x$ gives $5x+7$.

twin.prompt: Over $(x+4)(x+3)$, what is the collected numerator of $\frac{2}{x+4}+\frac{1}{x+3}$?
twin.explain: The 2 over $x+4$ needs $(x+3)$ and the 1 over $x+3$ needs $(x+4)$, so $2(x+3)+(x+4)=3x+10$. Each fraction's own bracket gives $3x+11$, and multiplying only the $x$ gives $3x+7$.

optionNotes.why: Each top was multiplied by its own bracket. A top needs the bracket it is missing: the 2 takes x + 3 and the 1 takes x + 4.
Only the x in each bracket was multiplied. The 2 multiplies every term of x + 3, so it gives 2x + 6, not 2x + 3.
Each top was multiplied by its own bracket. A top needs the bracket it is missing: the 3 takes x + 1 and the 2 takes x + 6.
The 3 and the 2 multiplied only the x inside each bracket. A number in front of a bracket multiplies every term: 3(x + 1) = 3x + 3.

noteBlocks.md: In the drawing, quarters and fifths cannot be added until both are cut into the same pieces, twentieths. Algebraic fractions work the same way: $\frac{4}{x+2}$ and $\frac{3}{x+7}$ are added only once both are counted in pieces of $\frac{1}{(x+2)(x+7)}$.

noteBlocks.title: Why adding tops and bottoms fails
noteBlocks.md: Adding the tops and adding the bottoms is not a rule at all. A number shows it: put the same value of $x$ into the question and into your answer. A right answer gives the same value both times; a wrong one does not.

steps.decision: Put $x=1$ into the question: $1+2=3$ and $1+7=8$, then add as ordinary fractions over 24.
Put x = 1 into the single fraction: the same value, because multiplying top and bottom by a bracket was multiplying by 1.
Adding tops and bottoms instead gives $\frac{7}{11}$ at $x=1$, not $\frac{41}{24}$, so it is not a method.

noteBlocks.prompt: Which of these has the same value as $\frac{5}{x-1}$ for every allowed $x$?
noteBlocks.explain: Multiplying the top and the bottom by the same bracket multiplies by 1, which is why See it gave $\frac{41}{24}$ both ways. Adding a bracket to both lines changes the value, as the $\frac{7}{11}$ showed, and multiplying only the bottom divides the fraction by $x+6$. So $\frac{5(x+6)}{(x-1)(x+6)}$.

twin.prompt: Which of these has the same value as $\frac{2}{x+4}$ for every allowed $x$?
twin.explain: Only multiplying the top and the bottom by the same bracket leaves the value alone. Adding a bracket to both lines changes it, and multiplying only the bottom divides the fraction by $x-3$. So $\frac{2(x-3)}{(x+4)(x-3)}$.

optionNotes.why: Adding the same bracket to the top and the bottom looks balanced, but only multiplying both by the same thing keeps the value.
The bottom gained x − 3 but the top did not, so the fraction was divided by x − 3. Multiply the top by it as well.
Adding the same bracket to the top and the bottom looks balanced, but only multiplying both by the same thing keeps a fraction's value.
The bottom gained the bracket but the top did not, so the fraction was divided by x + 6. Multiply the top as well.

noteBlocks.md: When the second fraction is taken away, all of its numerator is taken away. If that numerator has two terms, keep it in a bracket until the product is expanded, and only then remove the bracket.

noteBlocks.md: In the drawing the minus reaches every term: $-x^2$, then $+x$, then $+6$. Changing only the first sign is the slip that held most Summer 2025 candidates to three of the five marks.

noteBlocks.stem: Write $\dfrac{2x}{x+2}-\dfrac{x-3}{x+4}$ as a single fraction with a quadratic numerator.

steps.decision: Over the product of the brackets; the subtracted numerator has two terms, so it keeps its bracket.
Expand both products; the second stays inside its bracket, because the whole of it is being subtracted.
Now remove the bracket, changing every sign inside it, as in the drawing.
Collect: $2x^2-x^2=x^2$, $8x+x=9x$, and $+6$. The top is the quadratic the question asked for.

noteBlocks.explain: A minus before a bracket multiplies every term inside by $-1$, as step 3 of See it did: $-x^2$, then $+4x$, then $+7$. Collect: $5x^2-x^2=4x^2$ and $2x+4x=6x$. Changing only the first sign gives $4x^2-2x-7$, and keeping the last sign gives $4x^2+6x-7$. So $4x^2+6x+7$.

twin.explain: The minus changes every sign inside: $-x^2$, $+2x$, $+4$. Then $3x^2-x^2=2x^2$ and $5x+2x=7x$. Changing only the first sign gives $2x^2+3x-4$. So $2x^2+7x+4$.

optionNotes.why: Only the x² changed sign. The minus multiplies the whole bracket, so −2x becomes +2x and −4 becomes +4.
The x terms are right, but the −4 inside the bracket becomes +4 when the whole bracket is taken away.
Only the x² changed sign. The minus in front multiplies the whole bracket, so −4x becomes +4x and −7 becomes +7.
The x terms are right, but the −7 inside the bracket becomes +7 when the whole bracket is taken away.

noteBlocks.md: A whole number is a fraction over 1, so it joins the others over the common denominator: a number $n$ becomes $\frac{nD}{D}$, where $D$ is that denominator, because its top is $n$ times its bottom. Left outside, the answer is not a single fraction.

noteBlocks.title: Summer 2024, M4 Q18(b)
noteBlocks.md: Only about one candidate in ten earned full marks. Most combined the two fractions correctly, and the whole number was where it went wrong: it belongs over the common denominator too, not left outside.

steps.decision: The whole number goes over the common denominator: its top is the denominator itself.
All three tops over the one denominator; each fraction's top is multiplied by the bracket it lacks.

noteBlocks.prompt: Write $3+\frac{2}{x-5}$ as a single fraction. What is its numerator?
noteBlocks.explain: The 3 joins over the denominator as $\frac{3(x-5)}{x-5}$, as step 1 of See it wrote the 1 over the product. Then $3(x-5)+2=3x-13$. Adding the 3 to the 2 alone gives 5, and subtracting the 2 gives $3x-17$. So the numerator is $3x-13$.

twin.prompt: Write $2+\frac{5}{x-4}$ as a single fraction. What is its numerator?
twin.explain: The 2 joins as $\frac{2(x-4)}{x-4}$, then $2(x-4)+5=2x-3$. Adding the 2 to the 5 alone gives 7, and subtracting the 5 gives $2x-13$. So the numerator is $2x-3$.

optionNotes.why: The 2 was added straight onto the 5 as if it were already over x − 4. Write it as 2(x − 4) over (x − 4) first.
The 2 went over the denominator correctly, but the 5 is added, not taken away: 2x − 8 + 5 = 2x − 3.
The 3 was added to the top 2 as if it were already over x − 5. Write it as 3(x − 5) over (x − 5) first.
The 3 went over the denominator correctly, but the 2 is added, not taken away: 3x − 15 + 2.

noteBlocks.md: An equation lets you do what an expression does not: multiply both sides by the common denominator. Combine the left side first, then multiply every term, the number on the right included, by that denominator in one line. What is left has no fractions, and is usually a quadratic.

noteBlocks.md: In the drawing the line $y=2$ meets the curve twice, so expect two solutions. The curve breaks at $x=-2$ and $x=6$, where a denominator is zero, so neither can be an answer.

noteBlocks.stem: Solve $\dfrac{3}{x+2}+\dfrac{2}{x-6}=2$. Give your answers to 2 decimal places.

steps.decision: Combine the left side over the product, exactly as for an expression.
Multiply both sides by $(x+2)(x-6)$ in one line; the 2 on the right is multiplied too.
Expand each side on its own: $(x+2)(x-6)=x^2-4x-12$, then times 2.
Collect everything on the side that keeps $x^2$ positive.
No factor pair works, so the formula, with $-13$ in brackets before it is squared.
Both roots, to 2 decimal places. Neither is $-2$ or $6$, so both stand.

noteBlocks.title: Equations: Advanced Algebraic Fractions
noteBlocks.why: More equations cleared of their fractions and solved, at writing speed. Watch it once, then answer the checks without going back.

noteBlocks.prompt: Which line clears the fractions from $\frac{1}{x+4}+\frac{2}{x-3}=2$?
noteBlocks.explain: Multiplying both sides by $(x+4)(x-3)$ clears the left and multiplies the right, as step 2 of See it did: the 2 becomes $2(x+4)(x-3)$. Leaving the right as 2 multiplies only one side, and dropping the 2 loses a factor. So $(x-3)+2(x+4)=2(x+4)(x-3)$.

twin.prompt: Which line clears the fractions from $\frac{2}{x+5}+\frac{1}{x-1}=4$?
twin.explain: Every term is multiplied by $(x+5)(x-1)$: the tops by the brackets they lack, and the 4 by both brackets. Leaving the right as 4 multiplies one side only. So $2(x-1)+(x+5)=4(x+5)(x-1)$.

optionNotes.why: Only the left side was multiplied by the brackets. Whatever multiplies one side multiplies the other, so the 4 becomes 4(x + 5)(x − 1).
The right side took the brackets but lost its 4. The 4 stays as a factor: 4(x + 5)(x − 1).
Only the left side was multiplied by the brackets. Whatever multiplies one side multiplies the other, so the 2 becomes 2(x + 4)(x − 3).
The right side took the brackets but lost its 2. The 2 stays as a factor: 2(x + 4)(x − 3).

noteBlocks.prompt: An equation with no context gives $x=1.47$ and $x=-5.47$. What goes on the answer line?
noteBlocks.explain: Solve means every solution. A root is left out only when it makes a denominator zero or the context forbids it, and then the reason is written down, as step 6 of See it checked. Nothing rules either out here, so both: $x=1.47$ or $x=-5.47$.

twin.prompt: An equation with no context gives $x=0.62$ and $x=-3.12$. What goes on the answer line?
twin.explain: A negative root is still a root. With no context and no zero denominator to rule one out, both go on the line: $x=0.62$ or $x=-3.12$.

optionNotes.why: A negative root can feel wrong, but nothing here rules it out: no context and no zero denominator. Solve means every solution.
Dropping a root needs a reason from the question, and nothing rules out 0.62. Both values solve the equation.
A negative root can feel wrong, but nothing here rules it out: no context and no zero denominator. Solve means every solution.

noteBlocks.md: When the right-hand side is a fraction too, combine the left into one fraction first. Then there is one fraction on each side, and multiplying both sides by both denominators leaves each top times the other side's bottom.

noteBlocks.stem: Solve $\dfrac{3}{x+1}-\dfrac{2}{x+3}=\dfrac{1}{2}$. Give your answers to 2 decimal places.

steps.decision: Combine the left side; the subtracted top keeps its bracket until it is expanded.
Tidy the top: $3x+9-2x-2=x+7$.
One fraction on each side: each top times the other side's bottom.
Expand: $2x+14=x^2+4x+3$, then collect on the $x^2$ side.
Both roots to 2 decimal places; neither is $-1$ or $-3$.

noteBlocks.explain: One fraction on each side, so each top is multiplied by the other side's bottom, as step 3 of See it did. The 4 multiplies $x+7$, and the 1 multiplies the brackets: $4(x+7)=(x+2)(x+3)$. Putting the 4 on the brackets turns one side upside down, and $4(x+7)=1$ loses the brackets.

twin.explain: Each top times the other side's bottom: the 3 multiplies $x+9$ and the 1 multiplies the brackets. So $3(x+9)=(x+1)(x+5)$.

optionNotes.why: The 3 went onto the brackets, which turns one side upside down. Each top is multiplied by the other side's bottom, so the 3 multiplies x + 9.
The 3 is in the right place, but the brackets were lost from the right: the 1 multiplies (x + 1)(x + 5).
The 4 went onto the brackets, which turns one side upside down. Each top is multiplied by the other side's bottom, so the 4 multiplies x + 7.
The 4 is in the right place, but the brackets were lost from the right: the 1 multiplies (x + 2)(x + 3).

noteBlocks.md: Some questions give a story instead of an equation. Each fraction comes from one sentence: time is distance divided by speed, so a leg of $d$ km at $s$ km/h takes $\frac{d}{s}$ hours. The total time gives the right-hand side.

noteBlocks.md: Then solve as before. A root that makes a speed or a length negative is rejected, with the reason written beside it.

noteBlocks.stem: A walker covers 9 km at $x$ km/h, then 5 km at $(x-2)$ km/h. The walk takes 4 hours. Form an equation and find $x$.

steps.decision: Time is distance divided by speed for each leg; together they make the 4 hours.
Multiply every term by $x(x-2)$; the 4 is multiplied too.
Expand: $14x-18=4x^2-8x$, so $4x^2-22x+18=0$; then divide by 2.
Two numbers with product 18 and sum $-11$: $-9$ and $-2$, grouped as $(2x-9)(x-1)$.
$x=1$ would make the second speed $1-2=-1$ km/h, which is impossible, so it is rejected with that reason.

noteBlocks.prompt: Kai cycles 15 km at $x$ km/h, then 8 km at $(x+3)$ km/h. The ride takes 2 hours. Which equation?
noteBlocks.explain: Each leg's time is its distance divided by its speed, as step 1 of See it wrote: $\frac{15}{x}$ and $\frac{8}{x+3}$ hours, adding to 2. Distance times speed is not a time, and speed over distance is its reciprocal. So $\frac{15}{x}+\frac{8}{x+3}=2$.

twin.prompt: Ros rows 6 km at $x$ km/h, then 10 km at $(x-1)$ km/h, taking 5 hours. Which equation?
twin.explain: Time is distance divided by speed for each leg: $\frac{6}{x}$ and $\frac{10}{x-1}$ hours, adding to 5. So $\frac{6}{x}+\frac{10}{x-1}=5$.

optionNotes.why: Distance times speed is not a time. Time is distance divided by speed, so each leg gives a fraction.
That is speed divided by distance, the reciprocal of each time. Time is distance divided by speed.
Distance times speed is not a time. Time is distance divided by speed, so each leg gives a fraction.
That is speed divided by distance, the reciprocal of each time. Time is distance divided by speed.

noteBlocks.md: **"Give your answers to 2 decimal places."** Six of the seven fractional equations since November 2022 said this. It tells you the quadratic will not factorise into whole numbers, so go straight to the formula, bracket a negative $b$, and write both roots.
**A fraction on the right** (every November paper from 2022 to 2025). Combine the left side, then each top times the other side's bottom.
**A number or a fraction on the other side** (January 2020, Summer 2021, Summer 2023). Gather the fractions on one side first, so that one side is fractions and the other is a number.

noteBlocks.stem: Solve $\dfrac{2}{x-4}=3-\dfrac{1}{x+1}$. Give your answers to 2 decimal places.

steps.decision: Gather the fractions on one side first: add $\frac{1}{x+1}$ to both sides.
Now it is the familiar shape: combine and clear in one line, the 3 multiplied by both brackets.
Expand, $3x-2=3x^2-9x-12$, then collect on the $x^2$ side.
The formula, with $(-12)^2-4(3)(-10)=264$ under the root; both roots to 2 decimal places.

noteBlocks.prompt: Solve $\frac{5}{x+2}=4-\frac{3}{x-1}$. Which is the best first line?
noteBlocks.explain: Gather the fractions first, as step 1 of See it did: adding $\frac{3}{x-1}$ to both sides leaves fractions on one side and 4 on the other. Taking 3 from 4 treats the fraction as if its top were a whole number, and multiplying only some terms by $x-1$ unbalances the equation.

twin.prompt: Solve $\frac{4}{x+3}=2-\frac{1}{x-2}$. Which is the best first line?
twin.explain: Add $\frac{1}{x-2}$ to both sides so the fractions sit together and the 2 stands alone. Taking 1 from 2 treats a fraction as a whole number. So $\frac{4}{x+3}+\frac{1}{x-2}=2$.

optionNotes.why: Taking 1 from 2 treats the top of a fraction as a whole number. 1 over (x − 2) is not 1, so it cannot be taken from the 2 like that.
Only some terms were multiplied, which changes the equation. Gather the fractions on one side first, then multiply every term.
Taking 3 from 4 treats the top of a fraction as a whole number. 3 over (x − 1) is not 3, so it cannot be taken from the 4 like that.
Only some terms were multiplied by (x − 1), which changes the equation. Gather the fractions first, then multiply every term.

noteBlocks.md: **"Write as a single fraction"** (Summer 2024, Summer 2025). One fraction bar: the top expanded and collected, the bottom left as brackets. A whole number still outside, or the top set equal to 0, is not the answer.

Sometimes the single fraction is only the middle of the question: it is then multiplied or divided by another fraction (Summer 2019, November 2022), or the paper says simplify fully. Add first, over the product as always, then treat the result as one fraction.
Dividing is multiplying by the second fraction turned over. Then factorise every top and bottom, and cancel only whole brackets that appear above and below; a single term inside a sum never cancels.

steps.decision: Add the bracket first, over the product of its denominators.
Dividing by a fraction is multiplying by it turned over.
Factorise every part before cancelling: here a difference of two squares.
$(3x-5)$ and $(x-3)$ each appear above and below, so they cancel whole: one fraction bar, nothing left to cancel.

noteBlocks.prompt: The question says "write as a single fraction". Which of these is a finished answer?
noteBlocks.explain: A single fraction is one fraction bar, with the top collected and the bottom as brackets, as the last step of See it shows. The expression with 1 in front has the same value but is still two terms, and setting the top equal to 0 answers a question that was never asked.

twin.prompt: Asked for one fraction, which of these earns the last mark?
twin.explain: One fraction bar with the top collected is finished. The version with 2 in front is equal but still two terms, and an equation is not an expression.

optionNotes.why: It has the right value, but it is two terms, not one fraction. Write the 2 over the denominator and add the tops.
There was nothing to solve: the question asked for an expression. Setting the top equal to 0 turns it into an equation.
It has the right value, but it is two terms, not one fraction. Write the 1 over the denominator and add the tops.
There was nothing to solve: the question asked for an expression. Setting the top equal to 0 turns it into an equation.

noteBlocks.explain: Factorise first, as step 3 of See it did: $x^2-25=(x+5)(x-5)$. Then $(x+5)$ is above and below, so it cancels whole, leaving $\frac{x-5}{x-3}$. Keeping $x+5$ cancels the wrong bracket, and multiplying out the bottom hides the factor instead of cancelling it.

twin.explain: $x^2-49=(x+7)(x-7)$, and $(x-7)$ is above and below, so it cancels, leaving $\frac{x+7}{x+2}$. Multiplying out the bottom only hides the factor.

optionNotes.why: The wrong bracket stayed. x² − 49 = (x + 7)(x − 7), and it is (x − 7) that is also below, so it is (x + 7) that remains on top.
Multiplying out the bottom hides the shared factor instead of cancelling it. Factorise the top, then cancel the whole bracket (x − 7).
The wrong bracket stayed. x² − 25 = (x + 5)(x − 5), and it is (x + 5) that is also below, so it is (x − 5) that remains on top.
Multiplying out the bottom hides the shared factor instead of cancelling it. Factorise the top, then cancel the whole bracket (x + 5).

noteBlocks.text: Going further: a letter to find

noteBlocks.md: The hardest version (Summer 2022) tells you a solution and hides a letter in the denominators: an equation such as $\frac{p}{x+a}-\frac{q}{x-a}=1$ holds when $x$ is a given number, and you find $a$. Put the number in for $x$ first; then $a$ is the only unknown and the method is the one you know.

noteBlocks.title: Where the specification stops
noteBlocks.md: Every denominator here is linear. Fractions over a quadratic such as $x^2+3x+2$ are excluded from adding and from equations by the Teacher Guidance, and splitting a fraction into partial fractions is A level.

noteBlocks.stem: $\dfrac{4}{x+a}-\dfrac{6}{x-a}=1$ has the solution $x=4$. Find the possible values of $a$.

steps.decision: Put $x=4$ in first: now $a$ is the only letter.
Multiply every term by $(4+a)(4-a)$, the 1 included.
Collect on the $a^2$ side.
Two numbers with product $-24$ and sum $-10$: $-12$ and $2$.
Check each: neither makes $4+a$ or $4-a$ zero, so both stand.

noteBlocks.explain: Put $x=3$ in first, as step 1 of See it did: $\frac{6}{3+a}=\frac{2}{3}$. One fraction each side, so cross-multiply: $18=2(3+a)$, so $3+a=9$ and $a=6$. Check: $\frac{6}{9}=\frac{2}{3}$.

noteBlocks.md: Every line today used one rule: $\frac{a}{b}+\frac{c}{d}=\frac{ad+bc}{bd}$. It is not on the formula sheet, and it does not need to be, because it comes from multiplying by 1 twice.

steps.decision: Multiply the top and the bottom by $d$: that is multiplying by $\frac{d}{d}$, which is 1.
Multiply the top and the bottom by $b$ in the same way.
Both are now counted in pieces of $\frac{1}{bd}$, so the tops add and the bottom stays.
With $b=x+m$ and $d=x+n$, this is the line written in every See it above.

noteBlocks.prompt: By the same rule, what is the numerator of $\frac{p}{x+m}-\frac{q}{x+n}$ over $(x+m)(x+n)$?
noteBlocks.explain: Each top is multiplied by the other fraction's bottom, as steps 1 and 2 of See it multiplied $a$ by $d$ and $c$ by $b$: $p$ by $x+n$, $q$ by $x+m$, and the minus stays between them. Multiplying each top by its own bottom changes both values.

twin.prompt: By the same rule, what is the numerator of $\frac{r}{x+s}+\frac{t}{x+u}$ over $(x+s)(x+u)$?
twin.explain: Each top takes the other fraction's bottom: $r$ times $x+u$ and $t$ times $x+s$. So $r(x+u)+t(x+s)$.

optionNotes.why: Each top was multiplied by its own bottom. Each needs the other fraction's bottom: r takes x + u and t takes x + s.
Adding the tops alone works only when the bottoms already match. These differ, so each top is first multiplied by the other bottom.
Each top was multiplied by its own bottom. Each needs the other fraction's bottom, as a times d and c times b in the rule.
Subtracting the tops alone works only when the bottoms already match. These differ, so each top is first multiplied by the other bottom.

noteBlocks.md:
Put two linear fractions over the product of their brackets.
Keep a subtracted top in brackets; every sign changes as it goes.
Write a whole number over the common denominator too.
Clear an equation in one line and keep both roots unless one is ruled out.
Cross-multiply a fraction on the right; gather the fractions on one side first.

Almost every M4 paper ends with an equation like these, worth 6 to 8 marks and usually asking for 2 decimal places; some years add a single fraction worth 4 to 6. The first marks are for the common denominator with every top multiplied up; the last for both roots or the collected fraction. Stuck: write the two brackets as the denominator and bracket every numerator you subtract.

workedExamples.stem: Write $\dfrac{3x}{x+5} - \dfrac{x-2}{x+1}$ as a single fraction. Give your answer with a quadratic numerator and the denominator as a product of two brackets.

steps.decision: The two denominators are different linear brackets with no factor in common, so the lowest common denominator is their product. I leave it as brackets: expanding it earns nothing and the scheme accepts either form.
Each numerator is multiplied by the other denominator. The second numerator has two terms and is being subtracted, so it stays inside a bracket until it has been expanded.

options: Because the whole of (x − 2)(x + 5) is subtracted, not only its first term
Because a numerator must always be written in brackets
whyMenu.explain: The minus sign applies to the entire product; the bracket keeps it that way until the product has been expanded.

steps.decision: Each product is expanded on its own line. The subtracted one is still inside its bracket; nothing has been removed yet.
Minus a bracket changes every sign inside it: −x², −3x, +10. This is the line the Summer 2025 examiners said most candidates lost, by subtracting only the x².

options: −10, because a constant keeps its own sign
+10, because constants are always added at the end
whyMenu.explain: Every term in the bracket is multiplied by −1, so −10 becomes +10.

steps.decision: Collect like terms: 3x² − x² = 2x², 3x − 3x = 0, and +10. The numerator shares no factor with either bracket, so this is the finished single fraction.

twin.stem: Write $\dfrac{2x}{x+3} - \dfrac{x-1}{x+2}$ as a single fraction with a quadratic numerator.

workedExamples.stem: Write $3 + \dfrac{5}{x-2} - \dfrac{4}{2x+1}$ as a single fraction and simplify.

steps.decision: A whole number is a fraction with denominator 1, so it goes over the common denominator as well. Leaving the 3 outside is what held Summer 2024 Q18(b) to under a tenth full marks.

options: Because 3 = 3 ÷ 1, and multiplying top and bottom by (x − 2)(2x + 1) leaves its value unchanged
Because the 3 has to be added to each of the other numerators
Because whole numbers cancel with the denominators
whyMenu.explain: Multiplying numerator and denominator by the same expression is multiplying by 1, so the value of the 3 is unchanged.

steps.decision: All three numerators over the one denominator. The subtracted term keeps its bracket.
Expand the double bracket first, then multiply by 3. For −4(x − 2) the sign of the 8 flips: −4x + 8.
Collect: −9x + 10x − 4x = −3x and −6 + 5 + 8 = 7. The numerator does not factorise (b² − 4ac = 9 − 168 is negative), so nothing cancels.

twin.stem: Write $2 + \dfrac{3}{x+1} - \dfrac{1}{3x-2}$ as a single fraction and simplify.

steps.decision: Dividing by a fraction is multiplying by its reciprocal, so the second fraction is turned upside down. Nothing cancels yet. The November 2025 report said most candidates inverted and then stalled: the marks are in what comes next.
A difference of two squares. The number comes first in the expression, so the brackets keep that order: (7 + y)(7 − y). Writing (y + 7)(y − 7) would give y² − 49, the negative of what we have.

options: Because (7 + y)(7 − y) = 49 − y², while (y + 7)(y − 7) = y² − 49
Because the letter should always be written second
whyMenu.explain: Expanding both shows they differ by a sign; only (7 + y)(7 − y) equals 49 − y².

steps.decision: Every numerator and denominator is factorised before anything is cancelled; each of the other three has a common factor to take out.
Cancel whole factors only: (7 − y) with (7 − y), (y + 5) with (y + 5), y with y. What remains is (7 + y) over 2.

workedExamples.stem: Solve $\dfrac{5}{x+1} + \dfrac{2}{x-3} = 2$. Give your answers to 2 decimal places.

steps.decision: The left-hand side is combined over its common denominator exactly as for an expression. The = 2 waits on the right.

Both sides are multiplied by the denominator in one line: the left loses its denominator, the right becomes 2 × (x + 1)(x − 3). Every term on the right is multiplied. Summer 2024 Q23 candidates most often left the constant unmultiplied.

options: Whatever multiplies the whole of the left side must multiply the whole of the right side
The 2 is a numerator, so it collects the denominator
A denominator always moves to the other side as a divisor
whyMenu.explain: Multiplying both sides by (x + 1)(x − 3) keeps the equation balanced only if every term is multiplied.

steps.decision: The bracket product is expanded on its own line, then multiplied by 2. Brackets first, multiplier second.
Everything goes to the side that keeps x² positive: −4x − 7x = −11x and −6 + 13 = 7. Does it factorise? Pairs for 2 × 7 = 14 with sum −11: none. So the formula.
a = 2, b = −11, c = 7. Brackets around −11 before squaring: (−11)² = 121, not −121. This line is written before the calculator is touched.

options: So that −11 is squared to 121, rather than 11 squared and then negated
Because the formula sheet prints it that way
Because b is always negative in this topic
whyMenu.explain: A calculator reads −11² as −(11²) = −121; the brackets force (−11)² = 121.

steps.decision: √65 = 8.0623…, so (11 + 8.0623)/4 = 4.7656 and (11 − 8.0623)/4 = 0.7344. Both are answers: the question said solve, not find the positive value. Neither is −1 or 3, the values that would make a denominator zero.

twin.stem: Solve $\dfrac{4}{x+2} + \dfrac{3}{x-1} = 2$. Give your answers to 2 decimal places.

items.stem: What is the common denominator for $\dfrac{3}{x+4} + \dfrac{2}{x-1}$?
items.skill: Choose the common denominator for two linear denominators

options.feedback: The two brackets share no factor, so their product is the lowest common denominator. It can be left as brackets.
The denominators were added. Fractions with different denominators are combined over the product of the denominators; adding them gives nothing a marker can credit.
One denominator on its own does not divide by the other, so the second fraction cannot be rewritten over it. Use the product of both.

items.stem: $\dfrac{5}{x-2} - \dfrac{x+3}{x+1}$ is written over $(x-2)(x+1)$. Which numerator is correct?
items.skill: Form the numerators when subtracting, keeping a two-term numerator in brackets

options.feedback: Each numerator is multiplied by the other denominator, and the subtracted product is kept inside a bracket.
The second numerator must also be multiplied, by (x − 2). Only one part of the expression was multiplied up; the method mark needs both.
Each numerator was multiplied by its own denominator. To rewrite 5/(x − 2) over (x − 2)(x + 1), multiply top and bottom by (x + 1), the factor it is missing.
The bracket around (x + 3) has been lost, so the minus reaches only the x and the 3 is multiplied on its own. Keep (x + 3)(x − 2) together inside a bracket.

items.skill: Subtract a bracketed product, changing every sign

options.feedback: Only the x² was subtracted; the 3x and the −4 kept their signs. Minus a bracket changes every term: −x² − 3x + 4.
The −4 inside the bracket becomes +4 when the bracket is removed, because −(−4) = +4.

items.skill: Put a whole number over the common denominator

options.feedback: 4 = 4(x − 1)/(x − 1), so the numerator is 4x − 4 + 3 = 4x − 1.
The 4 was added to the numerator as if it were already over (x − 1). Write it as 4(x − 1)/(x − 1) first; that is the method mark.
4(x − 1) = 4x − 4; the −4 was lost. Multiply the whole bracket, then add the 3.
Adding 4 to the top and the bottom is not how a whole number joins a fraction. Put the 4 over the denominator (x − 1).

items.skill: Factorise top and bottom and cancel a whole factor

options.feedback: (x + 3)(x − 3) over (x + 3)(x + 2); the common factor (x + 3) cancels.
The x² terms were crossed out as if they were factors. Only whole factors cancel; factorise both parts before cancelling anything.
x² − 9 = (x + 3)(x − 3). The factor shared with the denominator is (x + 3), so the bracket left on top is (x − 3).
There is no equation here. The command is simplify: factorise and cancel to a fraction; setting the expression equal to zero earns nothing.

items.skill: Difference of two squares with the number first

options.feedback: Keep the order of the expression: 6² − p² = (6 + p)(6 − p).
That expands to p² − 36, the negative of what was given. The letter does not have to come first: (6 + p)(6 − p).
(6 − p)² = 36 − 12p + p², which has a middle term. A difference of two squares has one plus bracket and one minus bracket.

options.text: It does not factorise, because the number comes first
options.feedback: It does: 36 and p² are both squares. (6 + p)(6 − p) keeps the given order and expands back to 36 − p².

items.skill: Divide by inverting the second fraction, then cancel whole brackets

options.feedback: Invert and multiply: (x + 2)/(x − 1) × (x + 5)/(x + 2); the (x + 2) brackets cancel.
Inverted and multiplied correctly, but the common factor (x + 2) has not been cancelled. Simplify means finish: cancel every whole bracket that appears top and bottom.
The x on top and bottom of (x + 5)/(x − 1) are terms, not factors, so they cannot be cancelled. The fraction (x + 5)/(x − 1) is already in its simplest form.

items.stem: For $2x^2 - 11x + 7 = 0$, which is the correct expression under the square root in the quadratic formula?
items.skill: Substitute a negative b into the formula with brackets

options.feedback: −11² means −(11²) = −121. Bracket the negative: (−11)² = 121. A negative under the root here would wrongly suggest no solutions.
The formula has −4ac. With c = +7 that is −56, not +56.
c is +7; its sign was changed. Write a = 2, b = −11, c = 7 on a line of their own before substituting.

parts.stem:
Aoife cycles 12 km from home to the coast at an average speed of $x$ km/h. She cycles home by the same road at an average speed 5 km/h faster. The two journeys take 2 hours altogether.

Form an equation in $x$ and show that it simplifies to $x^2 - 7x - 30 = 0$.

scheme.for: time = distance ÷ speed used for at least one journey: 12/x or 12/(x + 5)
denominators cleared with every term multiplied: 12(x + 5) + 12x = 2x(x + 5)
24x + 60 = 2x² + 10x, then divided by 2 and rearranged to the printed equation with the working shown

The two times add to 2 hours: 12/x + 12/(x + 5) = 2.

context.setting: A boat on a river: 24 km upstream and back, current 2 km/h, 5 hours in all

A boat travels 24 km up a river and then 24 km back down. In still water its speed is $x$ km/h. The river flows at 2 km/h, so the boat's speed is $(x-2)$ km/h upstream and $(x+2)$ km/h downstream. The whole journey takes 5 hours.

Write the time taken for the upstream journey, in hours, as an expression in $x$.
hints: Time is distance divided by speed.

commonErrors.feedback: That is speed divided by distance, the reciprocal of the time. Time is distance divided by speed: 24 over (x − 2).

denominators cleared with every term multiplied: 24(x + 2) + 24(x − 2) = 5(x − 2)(x + 2)

Multiply every term by (x − 2)(x + 2), the 5 included.

The left side is $48x$ and the right side is $5x^2-20$, so $48x=5x^2-20$, which rearranges to $5x^2-48x-20=0$.

scheme.for: (5x + 2)(x − 10) = 0, or the formula with a = 5, b = −48, c = −20

x = 10 is one root; the equation also has x = −0.4. Solve means both: the context is used to choose between them in the next part, not here.

The bracket's top came out as 2x + 2: (x − 4) + (x + 2) = 2x − 2, since −4 + 2 = −2. With 2x − 2 it cancels with the 2x − 2 of the divisor, leaving (x + 4) over (x + 2).

questions.solutionProgram: 1/(x+2) + 1/(x-4) = (2x-2)/((x+2)(x-4)); divided by (2x-2)/(x^2-16) = (x+4)/(x+2); checked at sample points in the script

findTheMistake.stem: Cara was asked to write $\dfrac{4x}{x+1} - \dfrac{x-3}{x+2}$ as a single fraction with a quadratic numerator. Her working:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: (x − 3)(x + 1) = x² − 2x − 3, and the whole of it is subtracted. Cara subtracted only the x²: the −2x and −3 kept their signs instead of becoming +2x and +3.
findTheMistake.feedback: M1 A1 for the common denominator and the correctly bracketed numerators. Line 3 is where the marks stop: the product was never shown inside its bracket, so the sign change was applied to one term only. Expand inside the bracket on one line, remove it on the next with every sign changed, then collect. Summer 2025 M4 Q21: this slip capped most candidates at 3 of 5.

findTheMistake.stem: Dara was asked to solve $\dfrac{4}{x-1} - \dfrac{3}{x+2} = 1$, giving his answers to 2 decimal places. His working:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Multiplying by (x − 1)(x + 2) removed the denominator on the left, but the 1 on the right was not multiplied. The right-hand side should be (x − 1)(x + 2), which is why the quadratic never appeared.
findTheMistake.feedback: M1 A1 for combining the left-hand side. From line 2 nothing more can be credited: an equation with two algebraic denominators must produce a quadratic, and a linear answer is the signal to look back. A check would also have caught it: at x = −10 the left side is 4/(−11) − 3/(−8) ≈ 0.01, not 1. Summer 2024 M4 Q23: the constant on the other side was the term most often left unmultiplied.

findTheMistake.stem: Eimear was solving $\dfrac{3}{x-2} + \dfrac{1}{x+1} = 1$, giving her answers to 2 decimal places. Her working:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: b = −5, so b² is (−5)² = 25. Written as −5² the calculator squares 5 and then makes it negative, giving −25, so the discriminant came out as −13 instead of 25 + 12 = 37.
findTheMistake.feedback: Lines 1–4 are correct: M1 A1 for the setup, MA1 for clearing the denominators, MA1 for the quadratic. The formula line loses its mark and the final accuracy with it, 4 of 7. Bracket the negative before squaring, (−5)², and write the substitution before pressing anything. In this topic a negative under the root is almost always a slip to hunt for, not a conclusion. November 2025 M4 Q24: b² without brackets was the reported cause.

findings.asked: Solve an equation with two algebraic fractions that leads to a quadratic.
findings.wentWrong: Only the more able finished. Errors when expanding brackets and collecting terms, dropping the negative root, and not rounding to 2 d.p. Weaker candidates could not start.
findings.fullMarkAnswersDid: Combined the fractions over a common denominator, cross-multiplied to a quadratic, solved with the formula and gave both roots to 2 d.p.
findings.rule: Both roots count unless the context rules one out; round only at the end.

findings.asked: Write two algebraic fractions and a whole number as a single fraction.
findings.wentWrong: Under a tenth got full marks. Most combined the two fractions but had no idea what to do with the whole number.
findings.fullMarkAnswersDid: Wrote the whole number as (number x common denominator) / common denominator and combined all three numerators.
findings.rule: A whole number is a fraction with denominator 1 - put it over the common denominator too.

findings.asked: Solve an equation where the unknown is in the denominators.
findings.wentWrong: About a fifth got full marks. Common denominator and cross-multiplying were known, but the constant term was mishandled, fractions were moved across with wrong signs, and tidying up went wrong; most still reached a quadratic for some credit.
findings.fullMarkAnswersDid: Kept every term over one denominator, expanded carefully, and solved their quadratic (follow-through was available once most of the setup marks were earned and the roots were real).
findings.rule: Clear the denominators in one line, then expand with brackets before simplifying.

findings.asked: A standard fractional equation leading to a quadratic, with all the algebra on one side.
findings.wentWrong: One in five got full marks; most got the first two marks, then made errors expanding brackets and handling the constants. Some again ignored the negative root.
findings.rule: Write the expansion of every bracket as a separate line before collecting terms.

findings.asked: Add two algebraic fractions and simplify.
findings.wentWrong: Most got the common denominator and the first line, then subtracted only the first term of a multi-term numerator, capping them at 3 marks.
findings.fullMarkAnswersDid: Kept the subtracted numerator in brackets, expanded it fully with the sign applied to every term, then collected.
findings.rule: Minus a bracket changes every sign inside it.

findings.asked: Solve a fractional equation with algebraic denominators.
findings.wentWrong: Only top candidates finished; most set up the left-hand side correctly. Negative numbers caused trouble in expansions such as a multiple of (p - 1), and negative b was squared without brackets inside the quadratic formula.
findings.rule: Type (-b) in brackets when squaring in the quadratic formula.

findings.asked: Factorise the numerator and denominator of an algebraic fraction and simplify.
findings.wentWrong: About a third got full marks. Most took the common factor 2 out (some just divided by 2 instead), then partial credit for a difference of two squares. Weaker candidates cancelled single terms across the fraction or tried to solve it as an equation.
findings.rule: Only common factors cancel; an expression is simplified, never solved.

findings.asked: Factorise (grouping in the numerator, difference of two squares in the denominator) and cancel.
findings.wentWrong: Most got a mark for taking 3 out of the denominator. The difference of two squares went wrong when the letter was not the first term, because candidates swapped the terms round; grouping in the numerator troubled the less able.
findings.fullMarkAnswersDid: Kept the terms in their given order, wrote a squared minus b squared as (a + b)(a - b), and cancelled whole brackets.
findings.rule: 25 - w squared factorises as (5 + w)(5 - w) - do not reorder.

findings.asked: Divide one algebraic fraction by another and simplify.
findings.wentWrong: Only one in twenty finished. Most earned a mark or two for inverting the second fraction and factorising the denominators, then stalled.
findings.fullMarkAnswersDid: Inverted, factorised every numerator and denominator, cancelled the common brackets, and wrote the single remaining fraction.
findings.rule: Flip, factorise everything, cancel whole brackets.

insight.ruleToRemember: Put every term - including whole numbers - over the common denominator, keep subtracted numerators in brackets, cross-multiply to a quadratic, then give both roots (rejecting one only with a reason) rounded at the very end.
insight.aStarSignal: The unknown in two denominators with a constant elsewhere: cleared in one line, expanded without sign slips, and solved with the formula to 2 d.p. with both roots stated.
